newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa learns how to keep peace at military drill.
newsitem.headline: Africa learns how to keep peace at military drill.

text.p: The sound of gunfire rent the still African air, scattering a crowd of mourners who minutes before had been carrying to the burial grounds a relative who was shot in the head by rebel militias.

In seconds, United Nations soldiers who had been escorting the funeral procession, were swarming all over the area, diving for cover under the lush green grass as the sound of gunfire echoed around the African veld and a couple of tankers bore down towards the aggressors.
Moans filled the air, as several wounded children and old people who were too slow to take cover lay writhing in pain, begging for help.

Scenes from another African war? No, this the make-believe war-torn southern African country of Mycosa, part of an exercise by the region's soldiers learning how to work together and sharpen their skills to make and keep peace on their strife-ridden continent.

The operation, code-named Exercise Blue Hungwe (Fish Eagle), is the first ever African international peacekeeping exercise and observers say it could form the basis for a multinational peacekeeping force.

It involves 1,100 soldiers from Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania and Zimbabwe with help from the British Military Training and Advisory Team (BMATT) which boasts years of peacekeeping experience.

Personnel from U.N. agencies, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other aid organisations have also been involved to make the exercise in Zimbabwe's eastern district of Nyanga as close to reality as possible.
More than 100 villagers from the surrounding area and 200 soldiers playing two warring factions were also recruited to make Exercise Blue Hungwe realistic.

The operation -- which has been running from April 1 and ends on April 20 -- involved drills on such peacekeeping tasks as mine awareness, convoy protection, separation of warring factions, delivery of humanitarian aid and protection of refugees.

The exercise's chief controller, Zimbabwe National Army (ZNA)'s Major-General Mike Nyambuya said the joint programme had established a modus operandi for future cooperation in peacekeeping among the SADC countries and U.N. agencies.

"We have created and enhanced our inter-operabilities as forces from the SADC (Southern African Development Community) countries and forged a solid relationship which is a solid basis for the future," said Nyambuya, who served as deputy forces commander for the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Somalia.

He and senior officers from the region as well as the BMATT team were, however, quick to point out that the exercise was just a training one, dismissing suggestions that it was a preparation for a permanent regional peacekeeping force.
"This is very much a training stunt. This is the first time anybody has worked together like this," BMATT commander, Brigadier Adrian Naughten told reporters during a press briefing on the exercise.
ZNA Lieutenant-General Constantine Chiwenga said a permanent peacekeeping force would be too expensive to maintain.
Asked if there were plans to deploy the SADC force to war-torn Zaire in the event of a ceasefire, Chiwenga said this would be up to the politicians.
"What is important is that we should be able to prepare our forces and mobilise them quickly when the need for peacekeeping arises," he said.

SADC battallion commander Lieutenant-Colonel Lazarus Ncube of the ZNA said it was important that African armies be schooled and get involved in peacekeeping missions on the continent because they were better able to understand the problems of their region than foreigners.

"Our experience in Somalia showed us that people there tended to appreciate us more than forces from other parts of the world. We are Africans and we know our people, how they live and their problems," he said, adding that an African peacekeeping force, with a clear United Nations mandate, could have been more successful in Somalia.

Chiwenga said as a followup to Exercise Blue Hungwe, a SADC platoon commanders' course would be held in mid-June and a workshop on lessons learnt from Somalia was also planned for June, both in Zimbabwe.
